description: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding — electron transfer, sharing, dot-and-cross diagrams.
content_html:
Why Atoms Form Bonds

Atoms are most stable when their outer electron shell is full. Most atoms do not naturally have a full outer shell, so they bond with other atoms to achieve one. There are three main types of chemical bond: ionic bonding, covalent bonding and metallic bonding. All chemical bonds involve electrostatic forces — the attraction between opposite charges. The type of bond that forms depends on whether the bonding atoms are metals or non-metals.

Ionic Bonding

Ionic bonding occurs between a metal and a non-metal. The metal atom transfers one or more electrons to the non-metal atom. The metal loses electrons and becomes a positively charged ion (cation). The non-metal gains electrons and becomes a negatively charged ion (anion). The oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly — this electrostatic attraction is the ionic bond.

For example, in sodium chloride (NaCl): sodium (electronic configuration 2, 8, 1) loses one electron to become \(\text{Na}^+\) (2, 8). Chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains one electron to become \(\text{Cl}^-\) (2, 8, 8). Both now have full outer shells. In magnesium oxide (MgO): magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses two electrons to become \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), and oxygen (2, 6) gains two electrons to become \(\text{O}^{2-}\). In an ionic compound, vast numbers of ions pack together in a regular three-dimensional giant ionic lattice, where each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge.

Key Fact

In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred from metal to non-metal. The ions formed have opposite charges and attract each other. The compound forms a giant ionic lattice. You can use the charges of the ions to work out the formula — the charges must balance to zero overall.

Covalent Bonding

Covalent bonding occurs between non-metal atoms. Instead of transferring electrons, atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. Each shared pair of electrons forms one covalent bond. By sharing, both atoms achieve full outer shells. A single bond involves one shared pair; a double bond involves two shared pairs (e.g. \(O_2\), \(CO_2\)); a triple bond involves three shared pairs (e.g. \(N_2\)).

Examples: in water (\(H_2O\)), the oxygen atom forms a single covalent bond with each of two hydrogen atoms. In chlorine gas (\(Cl_2\)), two chlorine atoms share one pair of electrons. In carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)), the carbon forms a double bond with each oxygen atom. Covalent compounds range from small simple molecules (\(H_2O\), \(NH_3\), \(CH_4\)) to huge giant covalent structures such as diamond and graphite.

Dot-and-cross diagrams show the outer-shell electrons of each atom involved in bonding. Use dots (•) for electrons from one atom and crosses (×) for electrons from the other. For ionic bonding: draw the ions in separate sets of square brackets, show each ion’s charge, and show where the transferred electrons now sit. For covalent bonding: overlap the outer shells and show shared pairs in the overlap region. Common examples to practise: \(H_2\), \(Cl_2\), \(HCl\), \(H_2O\), \(NH_3\), \(CO_2\), NaCl, \(MgO\). These diagrams are models — they show electron arrangements but do not show the 3D shape, relative atom sizes, or bond lengths.

A dative covalent bond (also called a coordinate bond) is a special type of covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair come from the same atom. This occurs when one atom has a lone pair of electrons it can donate to another. An example is the ammonium ion (\(NH_4^+\)) formed when ammonia (\(NH_3\)) donates a lone pair of electrons to a hydrogen ion (\(H^+\)). The resulting bond is identical to any other covalent bond once formed; the distinction is only in how it was formed. Dative covalent bonds are assessed at Higher Tier only.

Metallic Bonding

In metals, atoms are arranged in a regular lattice structure. The outer-shell electrons leave their parent atoms and become delocalised — they are free to move throughout the whole structure. This creates a lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a “sea” of delocalised electrons. The strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the negative delocalised electrons holds the metal together. This is metallic bonding.

Key Fact

Metals conduct electricity because the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge through the structure. The same delocalised electrons allow metals to conduct heat. Metals are malleable (layers of positive ions can slide without breaking the bond, because the electron sea adjusts).

Predicting Bond Type from the Periodic Table

You can use an element’s position in the periodic table to predict what type of bond it will form. Metals are on the left and tend to lose electrons; non-metals are on the right and tend to gain or share electrons. A metal and a non-metal together → ionic bond. Two or more non-metals → covalent bond. A pure metal or alloy → metallic bond. Group number gives the outer electron count, and period number gives the number of shells — both are important in working out which atoms will bond and in what ratio.

The overall charge in an ionic compound must be zero. Group 1 metals form +1 ions; Group 2 metals form +2 ions. Group 6 non-metals form −2 ions; Group 7 non-metals form −1 ions. To work out the formula: find the lowest number of each ion that makes the charges cancel. For example, calcium (\(Ca^{2+}\)) and chloride (\(Cl^-\)): you need two \(Cl^-\) ions to balance one \(Ca^{2+}\), giving \(CaCl_2\). Aluminium (\(Al^{3+}\)) and oxide (\(O^{2-}\)): need 2 \(Al^{3+}\) and 3 \(O^{2-}\) for a total charge of zero, giving \(Al_2O_3\).
exam_tip_html: In dot-and-cross diagram questions, the most common errors are: (1) drawing ionic diagrams without square brackets and ion charges — these are essential; (2) showing covalent diagrams with electrons transferred rather than shared; (3) not showing all outer-shell electrons, only the bonding ones. For metallic bonding, always mention both the positive ion lattice and the sea of delocalised electrons — examiners expect both features. For questions asking you to predict bonding type, state metal/non-metal or non-metal/non-metal as your first step, then name the bond type.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionic bonding: electrons transferred from metal to non-metal, forming oppositely charged ions held in a giant lattice. Covalent bonding: electrons shared between non-metal atoms. Metallic bonding: delocalised electron sea holds a lattice of positive metal ions together.
  • Dot-and-cross diagrams show outer-shell electrons. Ionic diagrams require square brackets and ion charges. Covalent diagrams show shared pairs in the overlap between atoms.
  • Predict bond type from position in the periodic table: metal + non-metal → ionic; non-metal + non-metal → covalent; pure metal/alloy → metallic. Higher tier: dative covalent bonds form when both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom.

practice_questions.text:
Which statement correctly describes covalent bonding?
A) Electrons are transferred from a metal to a non-metal
B) A pair of electrons is shared between two non-metal atoms
C) Positive ions are surrounded by delocalised electrons
D) Electrons are transferred from a non-metal to a metal
practice_questions.marks: B) A pair of electrons is shared between two non-metal atoms [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the type of bonding present in a sample of pure copper.
Describe what happens to the electrons when magnesium and oxygen react to form magnesium oxide.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg2+ (cation). Oxygen gains two electrons to form O2- (anion). The oppositely charged ions attract each other.
Secure: Electron transfer described correctly with correct ion charges.
Developing: States that electrons move from magnesium to oxygen but does not give the resulting charges.
Emerging: Vague reference to electrons moving without direction or ion charges.

practice_questions.text: Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity but ionic compounds do not conduct electricity when solid.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Metals have delocalised electrons that are free to move through the structure and carry charge. In ionic compounds the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move, so charge cannot be carried. (Ionic compounds do conduct when molten or dissolved because ions then become free to move.)
Secure: Delocalised electrons in metals linked to conductivity; fixed ions in solid ionic lattice linked to non-conductivity.
Developing: Correct for metals or for ionic compounds but not both.
Emerging: General statement that metals conduct but no explanation linking structure.

practice_questions.text: Aluminium has atomic number 13. Draw the dot-and-cross diagram for aluminium chloride (AlCl3), showing the bonding clearly. State the type of bonding and give the charge on each ion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct ionic dot-and-cross diagram showing Al3+ in brackets with charge 3+ [1], each Cl- in brackets with charge 1- [1], all outer electrons shown for each ion [1], and correct overall formula AlCl3 with charges balancing to zero [1].
Secure: Three of the four marking points met.
Developing: Diagram drawn but brackets or ion charges missing.
Emerging: Electrons shown but type of bonding or ion charges incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Compare and contrast ionic bonding and covalent bonding. In your answer, describe how each type of bond forms, the particles involved, and give one example of a compound with each type of bonding.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Ionic — electrons transferred from metal to non-metal; forms positive and negative ions; held by electrostatic attraction in a giant lattice; example such as NaCl or MgO. Covalent — electrons shared between non-metal atoms; no charge transfer; molecules or giant structures; example such as H2O, CO2 or Cl2. Clear comparison of similarities (both involve electrostatic forces) and differences (transfer vs sharing; ions vs shared electrons).
Secure: Both types of bonding described accurately with an example each; some comparison made.
Developing: Both described but comparison is limited or one example missing.
Emerging: One type of bonding described only, or significant inaccuracies.

knowledge_checks.q: Which combination of elements forms an ionic compound?
What is the charge on a calcium ion formed when calcium bonds with a non-metal?
In covalent bonding, atoms achieve a full outer shell by _____ electrons.
The delocalised electrons in metals are free to move, which explains why metals are good conductors of _____.
Match each bonding type to the particles involved:
right: Metal and non-metal atoms — electrons transferred
Metal atoms — positive ions and delocalised electrons

flashcard_questions.q: What type of bonding occurs between a metal and a non-metal?
In ionic bonding, what happens to the electrons?
flashcard_questions.a: They are transferred from the metal atom to the non-metal atom.

flashcard_questions.q: What charge does a Group 1 metal ion have?
What charge does a Group 7 non-metal ion have?
What type of bonding occurs between non-metal atoms?
In covalent bonding, how do atoms achieve a full outer shell?
flashcard_questions.a: By sharing one or more pairs of electrons.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a double covalent bond?
flashcard_questions.a: A bond involving two shared pairs of electrons, e.g. in oxygen (O2) or carbon dioxide.
Electrons that are free to move throughout the metallic structure, not attached to any single atom.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are metals malleable (able to be bent and shaped)?
flashcard_questions.a: Layers of positive ions can slide over each other without breaking the bond because the electron sea adjusts.

flashcard_questions.q: What is shown in a dot-and-cross diagram for an ionic compound?
flashcard_questions.a: Each ion in square brackets with its charge, and all outer-shell electrons shown as dots or crosses.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula of calcium chloride, given Ca2+ and Cl-?
flashcard_questions.a: CaCl2 (two Cl- ions needed to balance one Ca2+).

glossary_terms.definition: A strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom.
A bond formed by the sharing of a pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
The strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons that holds the metallic structure together.
A compound consisting of positive and negative ions held together in a regular three-dimensional arrangement by strong electrostatic forces.
Diagrams showing the outer-shell electrons of bonded atoms using dots for one atom and crosses for the other, to illustrate how electrons are shared or transferred.
Electrons that are free to move throughout the metallic structure rather than being associated with any single atom.
